metadata.description: Definitions of hardware terms, technologies, and technical concepts.

data.definition: The general-purpose processor that executes program instructions.
data.short_explanation: The main general-purpose processor in a computer.
data.technical_explanation: A CPU fetches, decodes, and executes instructions using cores, caches, and execution units.
common_misconceptions: A CPU is not the same thing as a graphics card.

data.definition: A physical CPU execution complex.
data.short_explanation: Each core can execute its own instruction stream.
data.technical_explanation: A core contains execution units, registers, control logic, and cache resources.
common_misconceptions: A logical thread is not a full physical core.

data.definition: A schedulable stream of CPU work.
data.short_explanation: Threads are scheduled onto CPU execution resources.
data.technical_explanation: A software thread may run on a physical or logical processor.
common_misconceptions: A 16-thread CPU does not necessarily have 16 physical cores.

data.definition: Instructions per cycle.
data.short_explanation: A measure of how much work an architecture can complete per clock cycle.
data.technical_explanation: IPC varies with workload, architecture, cache behavior, and instruction mix.
common_misconceptions: Higher IPC is not the same as higher GHz.

data.definition: The frequency at which a processor operates.
data.short_explanation: Higher frequency can improve performance when other limits stay equal.
data.technical_explanation: Modern processors vary frequency dynamically based on power, temperature, and workload.
common_misconceptions: More GHz does not automatically mean a faster CPU.

data.definition: A processor's nominal reference frequency.
data.short_explanation: It is a baseline frequency rating.
data.technical_explanation: Actual operating frequency can move above or below this value.
common_misconceptions: The CPU does not always run at base clock.

data.definition: A higher frequency available under suitable conditions.
data.short_explanation: It is a dynamic performance frequency.
data.technical_explanation: Boost logic considers temperature, power, current, and workload.
common_misconceptions: A boost rating is not always an all-core guarantee.

data.definition: Simultaneous Multithreading.
data.short_explanation: A CPU core can expose multiple logical threads.
data.technical_explanation: Multiple thread contexts share many physical execution resources.
common_misconceptions: SMT does not double the number of physical cores.

data.definition: Intel's term for simultaneous multithreading.
data.short_explanation: It lets one physical core expose multiple logical processors.
data.technical_explanation: Hyper-Threading shares execution resources across hardware thread contexts.
common_misconceptions: Hyper-Threading does not create another complete core.

data.definition: A performance-focused CPU core.
data.short_explanation: It prioritizes high single-thread and latency-sensitive performance.
data.technical_explanation: Hybrid processors combine P-cores with efficiency cores.
common_misconceptions: P-core is not a separate CPU socket.

data.definition: An efficiency-focused CPU core.
data.short_explanation: It provides throughput with lower power per core.
data.technical_explanation: Hybrid CPUs use E-cores for background and highly parallel work.
common_misconceptions: E-cores are still real processor cores.

data.definition: A CPU design combining different core types.
data.short_explanation: Different core types target different performance and power goals.
data.technical_explanation: A scheduler assigns work across heterogeneous cores.
common_misconceptions: It is not the same as a dual-socket system.

data.definition: Thermal Design Power.
data.short_explanation: A thermal design target used for cooling and platform planning.
data.technical_explanation: TDP is not always equal to maximum electrical power consumption.
common_misconceptions: TDP is not simply the maximum wattage.

data.definition: Precision Boost Overdrive.
data.short_explanation: An AMD feature that expands allowed automatic boost limits.
data.technical_explanation: PBO can alter power and current limits while retaining automatic boost control.
common_misconceptions: PBO is not identical to fixed manual overclocking.

data.definition: An AMD tuning feature for voltage-frequency behavior.
data.short_explanation: It can improve efficiency or boost headroom.
data.technical_explanation: It applies voltage/frequency offsets on supported Ryzen processors.
common_misconceptions: A negative offset does not guarantee lower power in every workload.

data.definition: Hardware that predicts future control-flow decisions.
data.short_explanation: It helps keep CPU pipelines busy.
data.technical_explanation: Modern predictors use history and target structures to guess branches and targets.
common_misconceptions: Branch prediction is not perfect.

data.definition: A CPU technique that executes ready instructions before earlier blocked instructions.
data.short_explanation: It helps keep execution resources busy.
data.technical_explanation: Instructions execute according to dependency readiness and retire in architectural order.
common_misconceptions: It does not change program-visible ordering rules.

data.definition: A staged path used to process CPU instructions.
data.short_explanation: Multiple instructions can occupy different stages at once.
data.technical_explanation: Common stages include fetch, decode, execute, and retire.
common_misconceptions: A deeper pipeline is not automatically faster.

data.definition: A structure tracking in-flight out-of-order instructions.
data.short_explanation: It lets results retire in the correct order.
data.technical_explanation: The ROB holds instruction state until execution and exception conditions are complete.
common_misconceptions: ROB size is not the same as core count.

data.definition: The smallest and fastest common CPU cache level.
data.short_explanation: It stores frequently used data and instructions close to execution units.
data.technical_explanation: L1 is commonly split into instruction and data caches.
common_misconceptions: L1 is not system RAM.

data.definition: A CPU cache larger and usually slower than L1.
data.short_explanation: It reduces accesses to lower cache levels and DRAM.
data.technical_explanation: L2 may be private to a core or shared by a small core group.
common_misconceptions: More L2 does not guarantee more performance.

data.definition: A larger CPU cache often shared across cores.
data.short_explanation: It reduces accesses to system memory.
data.technical_explanation: L3 is slower than L1 and L2 but much faster than DRAM.
common_misconceptions: L3 size alone does not define CPU performance.

data.definition: The fixed-size unit transferred between cache levels.
data.short_explanation: Caches move data in blocks rather than individual bytes.
data.technical_explanation: A common modern cache-line size is 64 bytes.
common_misconceptions: Cache-line size is not cache capacity.

data.definition: Logic that manages communication between CPU and system RAM.
data.short_explanation: It handles memory channels and timings.
data.technical_explanation: Modern CPUs generally integrate the memory controller on the processor.
common_misconceptions: Older platforms often placed it in the chipset.

data.definition: AMD interconnect architecture connecting processor components.
data.short_explanation: It moves data between chiplets and platform components.
data.technical_explanation: Infinity Fabric links cores, I/O, and other processor blocks on AMD platforms.
common_misconceptions: It is not the same as CPU core clock.

data.definition: A smaller die combined with other dies in one package.
data.short_explanation: Chiplets allow scalable processor designs.
data.technical_explanation: A package can combine compute dies and I/O dies using high-speed interconnects.
common_misconceptions: Chiplet designs are not automatically slower than monolithic designs.

data.definition: Core Complex Die.
data.short_explanation: An AMD die containing CPU cores and cache.
data.technical_explanation: Zen desktop CPUs can use one or more CCDs connected to an I/O die.
common_misconceptions: CCD and IOD are different die roles.

data.definition: I/O Die.
data.short_explanation: An AMD die that handles memory and external I/O.
data.technical_explanation: It connects CCDs to memory and platform interfaces.
common_misconceptions: The IOD does not contain the normal CPU cores.

data.definition: System on Chip.
data.short_explanation: A chip integrating multiple major computing functions.
data.technical_explanation: A SoC can combine CPU, GPU, media, AI, memory, and I/O functions.
common_misconceptions: SoC does not mean low performance.

data.definition: A processor combining CPU and GPU resources.
data.short_explanation: It provides CPU cores and integrated graphics in one package or die.
data.technical_explanation: AMD uses the term APU for several integrated-graphics processor families.
common_misconceptions: APU is a product term, not a universal architecture.

data.definition: Neural Processing Unit.
data.short_explanation: A processor optimized for AI inference workloads.
data.technical_explanation: NPUs execute matrix and vector operations efficiently at low power.
common_misconceptions: NPU performance is not the same as gaming GPU performance.

data.definition: Tera Operations Per Second.
data.short_explanation: A theoretical AI throughput metric.
data.technical_explanation: TOPS depends on the operation type and numeric precision used.
common_misconceptions: TOPS is not directly comparable across all precisions.

data.definition: Floating-point operations per second.
data.short_explanation: A measure of floating-point compute throughput.
data.technical_explanation: It is commonly reported as GFLOPS or TFLOPS.
common_misconceptions: More TFLOPS does not automatically mean faster games.

data.definition: Graphics Processing Unit.
data.short_explanation: A processor optimized for highly parallel work.
data.technical_explanation: GPUs contain many execution resources designed to process large numbers of similar operations in parallel.
common_misconceptions: A GPU is more than a display controller.

data.definition: A board containing a GPU and supporting hardware.
data.short_explanation: It provides graphics processing, memory, power, cooling, and display output.
data.technical_explanation: A discrete graphics card typically includes the GPU, VRAM, PCB, VRM, cooler, firmware, and ports.
common_misconceptions: The GPU chip and graphics card are not technically identical terms.

data.definition: An NVIDIA shader execution unit term.
data.short_explanation: CUDA cores perform arithmetic work inside NVIDIA streaming multiprocessors.
data.technical_explanation: They are organized within SMs alongside special-function hardware.
common_misconceptions: CUDA cores are not directly comparable one-for-one with AMD stream processors.

data.definition: AMD's term for general shader execution units.
data.short_explanation: Stream processors perform arithmetic work in Radeon GPUs.
data.technical_explanation: They are organized into larger compute structures.
common_misconceptions: Stream processors are not equivalent one-for-one to CUDA cores.

data.definition: A specialized NVIDIA unit for matrix math.
data.short_explanation: It accelerates AI and deep-learning operations.
data.technical_explanation: Tensor cores perform high-throughput matrix operations used by AI features.
common_misconceptions: Tensor cores are not general CPU-like cores.

data.definition: A specialized NVIDIA ray-tracing accelerator.
data.short_explanation: It accelerates ray-primitive intersection work.
data.technical_explanation: RT cores handle dedicated ray-tracing operations while shaders perform additional work.
common_misconceptions: Ray tracing still uses shader resources.

data.definition: A major AMD GPU processing block.
data.short_explanation: It groups shader and related execution hardware.
data.technical_explanation: Modern AMD architectures organize shader resources into compute units or related structures.
common_misconceptions: A compute unit is not equivalent to a CPU core.

data.definition: NVIDIA GPU processing block containing execution resources.
data.short_explanation: SMs are the primary programmable processing blocks in NVIDIA GPUs.
data.technical_explanation: An SM includes CUDA cores, Tensor cores, registers, and other resources.
common_misconceptions: SM count alone does not determine performance.

data.definition: A GPU program that performs a rendering or compute task.
data.short_explanation: Shaders control how graphics are processed.
data.technical_explanation: Shader stages can include vertex, pixel, compute, and others.
common_misconceptions: A shader is software, not necessarily a physical core.

data.definition: Video Random Access Memory.
data.short_explanation: Dedicated memory used by a GPU.
data.technical_explanation: It stores textures, framebuffers, geometry, and other GPU-resident data.
common_misconceptions: VRAM is not the same as system RAM.

data.definition: A graphics memory standard.
data.short_explanation: It provides high-speed memory for GPUs.
data.technical_explanation: GDDR6 uses high-speed memory channels optimized for graphics bandwidth.
common_misconceptions: GDDR6 is a memory type, not a GPU architecture.

data.definition: A graphics memory technology using PAM4 signaling.
data.short_explanation: It provides higher bandwidth than conventional GDDR6.
data.technical_explanation: GDDR6X uses four-level signaling for higher transfer rates.
common_misconceptions: GDDR6X and GDDR6 are different technologies.

data.definition: A newer high-speed graphics memory standard.
data.short_explanation: It targets higher bandwidth and improved signaling efficiency.
data.technical_explanation: GDDR7 uses PAM3 signaling and newer memory-system techniques.
common_misconceptions: GDDR7 is not a GPU architecture name.

data.definition: The rate at which GPU memory can transfer data.
data.short_explanation: Higher bandwidth can help data-heavy workloads.
data.technical_explanation: Bandwidth depends mainly on memory data rate and bus width.
common_misconceptions: More VRAM capacity does not automatically mean more bandwidth.

data.definition: The width of the GPU-to-memory data interface.
data.short_explanation: Wider buses can move more bits per transfer cycle.
data.technical_explanation: Common widths include 128, 192, 256, and wider interfaces.
common_misconceptions: Wider is not automatically faster.

data.definition: A rendering technique that simulates light paths.
data.short_explanation: It can improve reflections, shadows, and lighting realism.
data.technical_explanation: Real-time ray tracing traces rays against scene geometry with hardware and software assistance.
common_misconceptions: Ray tracing can be used without full path tracing.

data.definition: A ray-tracing technique that follows many light paths.
data.short_explanation: It can produce highly realistic global lighting.
data.technical_explanation: Path tracing models light transport with many ray interactions and is computationally expensive.
common_misconceptions: Path tracing is generally more demanding than limited ray-traced effects.

data.definition: NVIDIA Deep Learning Super Sampling.
data.short_explanation: An AI-assisted reconstruction and upscaling technology.
data.technical_explanation: DLSS can reconstruct images and, in supported versions, generate additional frames.
common_misconceptions: DLSS is not just simple spatial scaling.

data.definition: AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution.
data.short_explanation: AMD's family of image upscaling and frame-generation technologies.
data.technical_explanation: Different FSR generations use different spatial, temporal, or frame-generation techniques.
common_misconceptions: FSR is not limited to AMD GPUs in every implementation.

data.definition: Intel Xe Super Sampling.
data.short_explanation: Intel's image upscaling technology.
data.technical_explanation: XeSS can use Intel XMX hardware or compatible DP4a execution paths.
common_misconceptions: XeSS can work beyond Intel Arc hardware.

data.definition: Render Output Unit.
data.short_explanation: A GPU block involved in final pixel operations.
data.technical_explanation: ROPs handle operations such as blending and framebuffer writes.
common_misconceptions: ROP count alone does not determine performance.

data.definition: Texture Mapping Unit.
data.short_explanation: A GPU unit that samples and filters textures.
data.technical_explanation: TMUs fetch texture data and apply filtering operations.
common_misconceptions: TMU count is only one performance factor.

data.definition: The process of converting geometry into fragments or pixels.
data.short_explanation: It is the traditional real-time graphics pipeline.
data.technical_explanation: Triangles are transformed into fragments before shading and final output.
common_misconceptions: Rasterization and ray tracing can be used together.

data.definition: Memory storing image data for display or rendering.
data.short_explanation: It holds rendered image information.
data.technical_explanation: A framebuffer can contain color, depth, and other buffers and is usually stored in VRAM on discrete GPUs.
common_misconceptions: The framebuffer is not the monitor itself.

data.definition: Image or data sampled by a graphics shader.
data.short_explanation: Textures provide surface and material information.
data.technical_explanation: Textures are stored in GPU memory and accessed through sampling hardware.
common_misconceptions: A texture is not always a color image.

data.definition: A tree structure used to accelerate ray-scene intersection.
data.short_explanation: It lets hardware skip groups of geometry that cannot be hit.
data.technical_explanation: BVHs organize primitives into nested bounding regions.
common_misconceptions: A BVH is an algorithmic data structure, not a GPU component.

data.definition: Rendering at lower resolution and reconstructing a higher-resolution image.
data.short_explanation: It can raise frame rate by reducing native shading work.
data.technical_explanation: Upscalers may use spatial, temporal, or AI reconstruction.
common_misconceptions: Upscaling quality depends strongly on input resolution and algorithm.

data.definition: A technique that synthesizes additional rendered frames.
data.short_explanation: It can increase displayed frame rate.
data.technical_explanation: The algorithm creates intermediate frames from prior frames and motion information.
common_misconceptions: Frame generation does not replace a healthy base frame rate.

data.definition: Resizable Base Address Register.
data.short_explanation: A PCIe feature allowing a larger GPU memory window to be mapped at once.
data.technical_explanation: It can reduce memory-window overhead in some workloads.
common_misconceptions: It does not add physical VRAM.

data.definition: Base Address Register.
data.short_explanation: A PCIe mechanism describing a device memory or I/O region.
data.technical_explanation: The OS maps device resources through BARs.
common_misconceptions: BAR is not physical storage.

data.definition: Random Access Memory.
data.short_explanation: Volatile system memory for active data and programs.
data.technical_explanation: RAM provides low-latency temporary storage for the operating system and applications.
common_misconceptions: RAM is not permanent storage.

data.definition: Fourth-generation DDR memory.
data.short_explanation: A common memory standard in older and many legacy PCs.
data.technical_explanation: DDR4 improves density and signaling over DDR3.
common_misconceptions: DDR4 is not electrically compatible with DDR5.

data.definition: Fifth-generation DDR memory.
data.short_explanation: A newer memory standard with higher data rates and new power management.
data.technical_explanation: DDR5 modules use onboard power management and two independent subchannels per DIMM.
common_misconceptions: DDR5 is not a faster DDR4 module.

data.definition: Dual Inline Memory Module.
data.short_explanation: A desktop memory module form factor.
data.technical_explanation: DIMMs use separate electrical contacts for memory signals.
common_misconceptions: DIMM describes form factor, not memory generation.

data.definition: Small Outline DIMM.
data.short_explanation: A compact memory module used in laptops and small PCs.
data.technical_explanation: SO-DIMMs reduce physical size compared with desktop DIMMs.
common_misconceptions: SO-DIMM is a form factor.

data.definition: An independent path between the memory controller and RAM.
data.short_explanation: Multiple channels increase memory bandwidth.
data.technical_explanation: Dual-channel platforms interleave traffic across two independent channels.
common_misconceptions: Two sticks do not automatically guarantee the intended channel mode.

data.definition: A memory configuration using two independent channels.
data.short_explanation: It increases theoretical memory bandwidth.
data.technical_explanation: The memory controller can interleave memory accesses across channels.
common_misconceptions: Dual-channel is different from dual-rank.

data.definition: Intel Extreme Memory Profile.
data.short_explanation: A profile system for configured RAM overclocking.
data.technical_explanation: XMP stores tested timing, frequency, and voltage settings in memory firmware.
common_misconceptions: XMP is not the same as JEDEC default settings.

data.definition: AMD Extended Profiles for Overclocking.
data.short_explanation: An AMD memory profile technology.
data.technical_explanation: EXPO stores tuned memory profiles for supported systems.
common_misconceptions: EXPO does not guarantee every kit will reach its rated speed on every CPU.

data.definition: The delay in clock cycles before a requested memory column becomes available.
data.short_explanation: Lower CAS can reduce latency when speed is comparable.
data.technical_explanation: Real latency depends on CAS value and actual memory clock.
common_misconceptions: Lower CL alone does not guarantee lower real latency.

data.definition: A set of parameters describing RAM access delays.
data.short_explanation: They describe how quickly memory responds to different operations.
data.technical_explanation: Common timings include CL, tRCD, tRP, and tRAS.
common_misconceptions: Timings must be considered with memory frequency.

data.definition: Error-Correcting Code memory.
data.short_explanation: Memory technology that can detect and correct some errors.
data.technical_explanation: ECC adds redundant information to detect and correct certain bit faults.
common_misconceptions: On-die ECC is not identical to system-level ECC.

data.definition: Registered DIMM.
data.short_explanation: A server memory module with register buffering.
data.technical_explanation: The register reduces electrical loading on the memory controller.
common_misconceptions: RDIMM is not normally compatible with consumer desktop boards.

data.definition: Load Reduced DIMM.
data.short_explanation: A server memory module using data buffers to reduce loading.
data.technical_explanation: LRDIMMs allow high-capacity memory configurations.
common_misconceptions: LRDIMM is different from RDIMM.

data.definition: A group of DRAM devices accessed as one logical unit.
data.short_explanation: Ranks affect memory organization and electrical loading.
data.technical_explanation: A DIMM can contain one or more ranks selected independently by the controller.
common_misconceptions: Rank is not the same as channel.

data.definition: An internal subdivision of DRAM storage.
data.short_explanation: Multiple banks allow parallel memory operations.
data.technical_explanation: Modern DRAM contains multiple banks and bank groups.
common_misconceptions: Bank and rank are different structures.

data.definition: Power Management Integrated Circuit.
data.short_explanation: A chip managing memory-module power conversion.
data.technical_explanation: DDR5 DIMMs commonly use onboard power management.
common_misconceptions: PMIC is not the memory controller.

data.definition: Error correction inside a DRAM chip.
data.short_explanation: It improves reliability inside the memory device.
data.technical_explanation: It corrects certain internal bit errors before data is exposed to the host.
common_misconceptions: On-die ECC does not provide full system ECC behavior.

data.definition: Firmware tuning performed during memory initialization.
data.short_explanation: It helps the motherboard find stable signal and timing parameters.
data.technical_explanation: Modern memory platforms may train after startup or configuration changes.
common_misconceptions: Long training time does not always indicate failure.

data.definition: A memory-controller mode with a 1:1 clock relationship on supported Intel platforms.
data.short_explanation: It can reduce memory-controller latency.
data.technical_explanation: The controller clock and memory clock run at the same effective relationship.
common_misconceptions: Gear modes are platform-specific.

data.definition: A memory-controller mode using a divided controller-to-memory clock relationship.
data.short_explanation: It can enable higher memory speeds.
data.technical_explanation: Higher memory frequency can come with additional controller latency.
common_misconceptions: Gear 2 does not mean half the memory speed.

data.definition: Solid State Drive.
data.short_explanation: A storage device using nonvolatile flash memory.
data.technical_explanation: An SSD combines NAND flash, a controller, firmware, and sometimes DRAM.
common_misconceptions: An SSD is not automatically NVMe.

data.definition: Hard Disk Drive.
data.short_explanation: A storage device using magnetic platters.
data.technical_explanation: Data is stored magnetically and accessed by moving heads.
common_misconceptions: Capacity alone does not describe HDD speed.

data.definition: Non-Volatile Memory Express.
data.short_explanation: A storage protocol designed for PCIe-connected flash storage.
data.technical_explanation: NVMe supports many parallel queues and lower protocol overhead than SATA AHCI.
common_misconceptions: NVMe is a protocol, not a connector.

data.definition: Serial ATA.
data.short_explanation: A storage interface standard.
data.technical_explanation: SATA provides serial point-to-point storage communication.
common_misconceptions: SATA data and SATA power are separate connectors.

data.definition: A nonvolatile semiconductor memory technology.
data.short_explanation: It stores data without continuous power.
data.technical_explanation: SSD controllers manage NAND pages, blocks, wear, and error correction.
common_misconceptions: NAND is not the whole SSD.

data.definition: Single-Level Cell flash.
data.short_explanation: NAND that stores one bit per cell.
data.technical_explanation: It provides high endurance and low latency at low density.
common_misconceptions: Consumer SSDs rarely use pure SLC for bulk capacity.

data.definition: Multi-Level Cell flash storing two bits per cell.
data.short_explanation: It balances density and endurance.
data.technical_explanation: MLC was common in earlier enthusiast and enterprise SSDs.
common_misconceptions: MLC has been largely displaced in consumer SSDs.

data.definition: Triple-Level Cell flash storing three bits per cell.
data.short_explanation: A common balance of cost, capacity, and endurance.
data.technical_explanation: TLC SSDs often use dynamic SLC caching for burst writes.
common_misconceptions: TLC is not always faster than every MLC product.

data.definition: Quad-Level Cell flash storing four bits per cell.
data.short_explanation: It increases density and lowers cost per GB.
data.technical_explanation: QLC can have lower endurance and sustained write performance than higher-endurance NAND types.
common_misconceptions: QLC can be excellent for many consumer workloads.

data.definition: Volatile memory used by some SSD controllers for metadata.
data.short_explanation: It can improve mapping and random-access behavior.
data.technical_explanation: The SSD may cache flash translation layer metadata in DRAM.
common_misconceptions: A DRAMless SSD can still be fast.

data.definition: Host Memory Buffer.
data.short_explanation: A feature allowing an NVMe SSD to use system RAM for metadata.
data.technical_explanation: It provides a DRAMless SSD with a host-side metadata cache.
common_misconceptions: HMB does not turn system RAM into full SSD DRAM.

data.definition: Flash Translation Layer.
data.short_explanation: The SSD control software mapping logical addresses to NAND locations.
data.technical_explanation: The FTL handles wear leveling, garbage collection, bad-block management, and mapping.
common_misconceptions: The FTL is not a filesystem.

data.definition: Terabytes Written.
data.short_explanation: An SSD endurance rating expressed as total written data.
data.technical_explanation: Manufacturers use TBW to describe expected endurance over a warranty period.
common_misconceptions: TBW is a rating, not an exact failure point.

data.definition: Drive Writes Per Day.
data.short_explanation: An enterprise endurance metric based on full-drive writes per day.
data.technical_explanation: It is defined over a stated service or warranty period.
common_misconceptions: DWPD only has meaning with the specified period and capacity.

data.definition: Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology.
data.short_explanation: A storage health and telemetry system.
data.technical_explanation: SMART exposes attributes such as temperature, wear, errors, and operating hours.
common_misconceptions: SMART cannot predict every failure.

data.definition: A portion of NAND operated as pseudo-SLC for faster writes.
data.short_explanation: It boosts short bursts of write performance.
data.technical_explanation: The controller later folds cached data into denser NAND states.
common_misconceptions: SLC cache can shrink as free space decreases.

data.definition: SSD maintenance that consolidates valid pages and erases blocks.
data.short_explanation: It creates reusable flash space.
data.technical_explanation: Controllers move valid data and erase blocks that contain stale pages.
common_misconceptions: Garbage collection is normal SSD behavior.

data.definition: A command allowing the OS to mark deleted SSD blocks as no longer needed.
data.short_explanation: It improves future write efficiency.
data.technical_explanation: The controller can reclaim NAND pages earlier when unused blocks are reported.
common_misconceptions: TRIM is not secure erase.

data.definition: A technique distributing writes across flash blocks.
data.short_explanation: It helps spread NAND wear.
data.technical_explanation: Controllers rotate write locations to prevent a small set of blocks from wearing out early.
common_misconceptions: Wear leveling cannot eliminate flash wear.

data.definition: The ratio of physical NAND writes to host writes.
data.short_explanation: Lower write amplification improves endurance and efficiency.
data.technical_explanation: Garbage collection, data movement, and metadata can cause extra writes.
common_misconceptions: Write amplification depends heavily on workload.

data.definition: A magnetic disk inside an HDD.
data.short_explanation: It is the surface that stores magnetic data.
data.technical_explanation: An HDD can contain multiple platters mounted on a spindle.
common_misconceptions: A platter is only one part of an HDD.

data.definition: The mechanism positioning an HDD read/write head.
data.short_explanation: It moves heads across disk tracks.
data.technical_explanation: A voice-coil actuator moves the head assembly accurately across platters.
common_misconceptions: The actuator does not spin the disk.

data.definition: The time for an HDD head to move to a target track.
data.short_explanation: Lower seek time improves random-access response.
data.technical_explanation: It is one component of total storage access latency.
common_misconceptions: Seek time is not transfer speed.

data.definition: A logical unit of storage addressing.
data.short_explanation: Storage devices expose data in fixed-size sectors or logical blocks.
data.technical_explanation: Common logical sector sizes include 512 bytes and 4096 bytes.
common_misconceptions: Physical and logical sector size can differ.

data.definition: Logical Block Addressing.
data.short_explanation: A numbering scheme for storage blocks.
data.technical_explanation: Modern drives expose a linear sequence of logical block addresses to the host.
common_misconceptions: LBA does not describe physical disk geometry.

data.definition: A storage format using 4096-byte logical sectors.
data.short_explanation: The host sees native 4K logical blocks.
data.technical_explanation: 4Kn can improve metadata efficiency but requires compatible software.
common_misconceptions: 4Kn is different from 512e.

data.definition: A drive using 512-byte logical sectors over 4096-byte physical sectors.
data.short_explanation: It preserves compatibility with older software.
data.technical_explanation: The drive emulates 512-byte logical blocks over 4K physical sectors.
common_misconceptions: The physical sector is still 4K.

data.definition: Redundant Array of Independent Disks.
data.short_explanation: A method of combining multiple drives for performance, capacity, or redundancy.
data.technical_explanation: Different RAID levels use striping, mirroring, and parity in different ways.
common_misconceptions: RAID is not a backup.

data.definition: A striped RAID layout with no redundancy.
data.short_explanation: It increases aggregate throughput and capacity.
data.technical_explanation: Data is distributed across members and any member failure can destroy the array.
common_misconceptions: RAID 0 has no fault tolerance.

data.definition: A mirrored RAID layout.
data.short_explanation: It duplicates data across drives.
data.technical_explanation: A mirrored set can survive a member failure in common two-drive configurations.
common_misconceptions: Usable capacity is lower than total raw capacity.

data.definition: Striped storage with distributed parity.
data.short_explanation: It tolerates one drive failure in a typical implementation.
data.technical_explanation: Parity allows the missing member data to be reconstructed.
common_misconceptions: RAID 5 is not ideal for every large modern array.

data.definition: Striped storage with dual distributed parity.
data.short_explanation: It can tolerate two member failures.
data.technical_explanation: Two independent parity calculations provide extra fault tolerance.
common_misconceptions: It requires more parity capacity than RAID 5.

data.definition: A mirrored and striped RAID layout.
data.short_explanation: It combines redundancy and performance.
data.technical_explanation: Data is mirrored in pairs and then striped across those mirrors.
common_misconceptions: RAID 10 is not the same as RAID 01.

data.definition: Redundant information used to reconstruct missing data.
data.short_explanation: It enables fault tolerance in systems like RAID.
data.technical_explanation: Parity is calculated from data using mathematical operations.
common_misconceptions: Parity is not a second copy of the data.

data.definition: A separate copy of data kept for recovery.
data.short_explanation: It protects against deletion, corruption, and hardware loss.
data.technical_explanation: Backups should be independent from the primary storage system.
common_misconceptions: RAID alone is not a backup.

data.definition: A point-in-time logical view of stored data.
data.short_explanation: It captures the state of a storage system at a moment.
data.technical_explanation: Copy-on-write metadata can preserve access to unchanged blocks.
common_misconceptions: A snapshot may depend on the original storage system.

data.definition: A copy of a drive or storage layout.
data.short_explanation: It can be used for migration or duplication.
data.technical_explanation: Cloning may copy filesystems, partitions, or raw blocks depending on the tool.
common_misconceptions: A clone is not always an archival backup.

data.definition: A structure for organizing files on storage.
data.short_explanation: It controls how files and metadata are stored.
data.technical_explanation: Filesystems manage allocation, directories, metadata, and permissions.
common_misconceptions: A filesystem is not the same thing as a partition.

data.definition: Windows filesystem supporting permissions and journaling.
data.short_explanation: It is the common Windows filesystem for system and data volumes.
data.technical_explanation: NTFS stores file metadata and allocation information in filesystem structures.
common_misconceptions: Windows can access other filesystem types too.

data.definition: A common Linux filesystem.
data.short_explanation: It supports journaling, extents, and large volumes.
data.technical_explanation: ext4 manages files and allocation through inode and block structures.
common_misconceptions: Not every Linux installation uses ext4.

data.definition: Apple File System.
data.short_explanation: A filesystem designed for modern Apple operating systems.
data.technical_explanation: APFS supports snapshots, cloning, encryption, and copy-on-write techniques.
common_misconceptions: APFS is not identical to HFS+.

data.definition: A logical region of a storage device.
data.short_explanation: It divides a disk into independently managed areas.
data.technical_explanation: Partition tables define boundaries, identifiers, and attributes.
common_misconceptions: A partition is not the same as a filesystem.

data.definition: GUID Partition Table.
data.short_explanation: A modern partition-table format.
data.technical_explanation: GPT supports large disks and many partitions and stores redundant metadata.
common_misconceptions: GPT is not a filesystem.

data.definition: Master Boot Record.
data.short_explanation: A legacy partition table and boot format.
data.technical_explanation: MBR stores partition information and legacy boot code near the start of a disk.
common_misconceptions: MBR is not the same thing as BIOS.

data.definition: A small partition used by UEFI bootloaders.
data.short_explanation: It stores files required for firmware-based booting.
data.technical_explanation: The ESP commonly uses FAT and contains an EFI directory hierarchy.
common_misconceptions: The ESP is not normally for user documents.

data.definition: A 24-contact reversible USB connector used for data, power, and alternate modes.
data.short_explanation: It is the modern reversible USB connector.
data.technical_explanation: The same connector can carry USB, DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt, and USB Power Delivery when supported.
common_misconceptions: The connector shape alone does not identify speed.

data.definition: A standard rectangular USB host connector.
data.short_explanation: It remains common on desktops and peripherals.
data.technical_explanation: Type-A connectors are used across multiple USB generations.
common_misconceptions: Type-A does not imply USB 2.0.

data.definition: A traditional peripheral-side USB connector.
data.short_explanation: It is common on printers and some audio devices.
data.technical_explanation: Type-B exists in several physical variants across USB generations.
common_misconceptions: Type-B is not one single connector for every USB version.

data.definition: A compact USB peripheral connector.
data.short_explanation: It was widely used on older phones and devices.
data.technical_explanation: Micro-B commonly carries USB 2.0 signaling.
common_misconceptions: Micro-B is not USB Type-C.

data.definition: A wider micro connector used on many external drives.
data.short_explanation: It provides SuperSpeed USB connections to storage.
data.technical_explanation: The connector contains separate USB 3.x SuperSpeed contacts alongside USB 2.0 contacts.
common_misconceptions: It is physically different from standard Micro-B USB 2.0.

data.definition: A connector used to carry DisplayPort video and audio.
data.short_explanation: It is common on desktop GPUs and monitors.
data.technical_explanation: The connector carries differential high-speed lanes and auxiliary signaling.
common_misconceptions: Connector shape does not prove the DisplayPort revision.

data.definition: A smaller DisplayPort connector.
data.short_explanation: It was common on laptops and earlier Thunderbolt devices.
data.technical_explanation: Mini DisplayPort uses the DisplayPort signaling family in a compact form factor.
common_misconceptions: Mini DisplayPort is not Mini HDMI.

data.definition: The standard full-size HDMI connector.
data.short_explanation: It is used for TVs, monitors, and GPUs.
data.technical_explanation: It has 19 contacts and carries audio and video.
common_misconceptions: The connector does not guarantee HDMI 2.1 features.

data.definition: The common modular connector used for twisted-pair Ethernet.
data.short_explanation: It is the familiar Ethernet network plug.
data.technical_explanation: The plug is commonly an 8P8C modular connector used by many Ethernet standards.
common_misconceptions: RJ45 and 8P8C are related terms but not literally identical standards.

data.definition: A small pluggable transceiver interface for 10Gb-class links.
data.short_explanation: It is common on switches and network adapters.
data.technical_explanation: SFP+ uses a compact pluggable cage that can accept optical or copper transceivers.
common_misconceptions: SFP+ itself is the cage and interface, not the optical medium.

data.definition: A quad-lane pluggable transceiver interface associated with 100Gb-class links.
data.short_explanation: It is common in datacenter networking.
data.technical_explanation: QSFP28 aggregates multiple high-speed lanes in one module.
common_misconceptions: QSFP28 is not the same as SFP28.

data.definition: A three-contact analog audio plug or jack.
data.short_explanation: It commonly carries stereo audio.
data.technical_explanation: Tip, ring, and sleeve contacts support stereo or balanced applications depending on wiring.
common_misconceptions: 3.5mm TRS is not always stereo in every wiring scheme.

data.definition: A four-contact analog headset connector.
data.short_explanation: It can carry stereo audio plus microphone.
data.technical_explanation: CTIA and OMTP use different contact assignments.
common_misconceptions: TRRS pin assignments can differ.

data.definition: An optical digital audio connection.
data.short_explanation: It carries S/PDIF audio over light.
data.technical_explanation: A plastic or glass optical fiber carries the encoded digital audio stream.
common_misconceptions: TOSLINK is a physical interface, while S/PDIF is the signal format.

data.definition: A coaxial analog connector used for audio and video.
data.short_explanation: It is common on legacy AV hardware.
data.technical_explanation: RCA connectors carry one signal per connector and can be analog or digital depending on use.
common_misconceptions: RCA describes the connector type, not one protocol.

data.definition: A 6-pin mini-DIN connector for legacy keyboards and mice.
data.short_explanation: It provides dedicated keyboard or mouse connections.
data.technical_explanation: PS/2 is a low-speed serial interface with dedicated signal and power pins.
common_misconceptions: PS/2 is not a USB connector.

data.definition: A 9-contact D-sub connector used for serial and other legacy interfaces.
data.short_explanation: It is commonly called DB-9 in PC discussions.
data.technical_explanation: DE-9 is the precise shell-size designation for the 9-contact D-sub connector.
common_misconceptions: DB-9 is a common but technically imprecise name for DE-9.

data.definition: A 25-contact D-sub connector used for parallel and serial interfaces.
data.short_explanation: It was common on legacy PCs and printers.
data.technical_explanation: Different protocols can use DB-25 with different pin assignments.
common_misconceptions: The connector alone does not identify the protocol.

data.definition: The input/output path between a system and external or attached devices.
data.short_explanation: I/O covers data moving into or out of the processor and memory system.
data.technical_explanation: I/O can use buses, DMA, interrupts, and controllers to move data between devices and memory.
common_misconceptions: I/O is broader than just storage.

data.definition: A signal or event requesting CPU attention.
data.short_explanation: Interrupts let hardware notify software of important events.
data.technical_explanation: The processor records state and transfers control to an interrupt handler or vector.
common_misconceptions: An interrupt does not always stop all CPU execution globally.

data.definition: Repeatedly checking a device or status value for a condition.
data.short_explanation: It is an alternative to interrupts for monitoring events.
data.technical_explanation: Software reads a status register repeatedly until an event occurs or a timeout expires.
common_misconceptions: Polling can waste CPU time if used inefficiently.

data.definition: Changing CPU execution from one thread or process to another.
data.short_explanation: The OS saves one execution context and loads another.
data.technical_explanation: Context switches can involve registers, scheduling state, and memory-management state.
common_misconceptions: A context switch is not necessarily expensive in every case.

data.definition: An operating-system instance of a running program.
data.short_explanation: A process owns resources and contains one or more threads.
data.technical_explanation: Processes have virtual address spaces and operating-system-managed handles and permissions.
common_misconceptions: A process is not the same as a single thread.

data.definition: Running or representing computing resources in software-defined environments.
data.short_explanation: It lets multiple workloads share one physical machine.
data.technical_explanation: A hypervisor virtualizes CPU, memory, storage, and I/O resources.
common_misconceptions: Virtualization is broader than virtual machines.

data.definition: An isolated application environment sharing the host kernel.
data.short_explanation: Containers package software and dependencies with less overhead than full VMs.
data.technical_explanation: Namespaces, cgroups, and filesystem isolation provide container boundaries on Linux.
common_misconceptions: Containers are not full hardware virtual machines.

data.definition: Using a GPU for non-graphics parallel computation.
data.short_explanation: GPUs can accelerate scientific, AI, and media workloads.
data.technical_explanation: Compute APIs map parallel kernels onto GPU execution resources.
common_misconceptions: GPU compute is not limited to gaming.

data.definition: NVIDIA parallel computing platform and programming model.
data.short_explanation: It lets applications use NVIDIA GPUs for general-purpose compute.
data.technical_explanation: CUDA exposes kernels, memory spaces, streams, and device APIs.
common_misconceptions: CUDA is NVIDIA-specific.

data.definition: An open standard for heterogeneous compute.
data.short_explanation: It can run compute kernels across CPUs, GPUs, and other devices.
data.technical_explanation: OpenCL separates host code from device kernels and uses explicit memory and command queues.
common_misconceptions: OpenCL is not the same as OpenGL.

data.definition: A DirectX compute API for general-purpose GPU workloads.
data.short_explanation: It lets Windows applications run compute shaders.
data.technical_explanation: DirectCompute integrates compute workloads into the Direct3D ecosystem.
common_misconceptions: DirectCompute is not the same as Direct3D rendering.

data.definition: A GPU shader stage designed for general computation.
data.short_explanation: It performs parallel workloads outside traditional graphics stages.
data.technical_explanation: Compute shaders use thread groups and shared resources for arbitrary data processing.
common_misconceptions: A compute shader is software, not a physical hardware core.

data.definition: A group of GPU threads executed or scheduled together.
data.short_explanation: It lets compute workloads share local resources.
data.technical_explanation: APIs such as Vulkan and DirectX divide compute work into thread groups or workgroups.
common_misconceptions: A workgroup is not the same thing as a GPU execution unit.

data.definition: A group of NVIDIA GPU threads executed together in SIMD/SIMT style.
data.short_explanation: NVIDIA GPUs schedule threads in warps.
data.technical_explanation: A warp commonly contains 32 threads on modern NVIDIA architectures.
common_misconceptions: A warp is not equivalent to one CUDA core.

data.definition: A group of GPU threads processed together on AMD architectures.
data.short_explanation: It is AMD's SIMD execution grouping.
data.technical_explanation: Wavefront size depends on architecture and can differ from warp terminology.
common_misconceptions: Wavefront and warp are similar concepts but not identical implementation details.

data.definition: Single Instruction, Multiple Threads.
data.short_explanation: A GPU execution model where groups of threads follow common instructions.
data.technical_explanation: Threads execute in groups while maintaining individual data and control state.
common_misconceptions: SIMT is not identical to classic CPU SIMD.

data.definition: Single Instruction, Multiple Data.
data.short_explanation: A method applying one instruction to multiple data elements.
data.technical_explanation: Vector instructions allow one instruction to operate on multiple lanes of data.
common_misconceptions: SIMD and SIMT use different execution models.

data.definition: Streaming SIMD Extensions.
data.short_explanation: A family of x86 vector instruction extensions.
data.technical_explanation: SSE provides vector operations for floating-point and integer workloads.
common_misconceptions: SSE instructions are not exclusive to Intel CPUs.

data.definition: Advanced Vector Extensions.
data.short_explanation: An x86 vector instruction set extension.
data.technical_explanation: AVX widens vector operations and improves parallel arithmetic throughput.
common_misconceptions: AVX is not a CPU architecture.

data.definition: An x86 vector instruction extension adding wider integer operations and FMA support with suitable instructions.
data.short_explanation: It expands SIMD compute capability.
data.technical_explanation: AVX2 uses 256-bit integer vectors and works with FMA3 on supporting CPUs.
common_misconceptions: AVX2 support does not imply AVX-512 support.

data.definition: A family of x86 vector instruction extensions using 512-bit registers and related features.
data.short_explanation: It enables wider vector operations on supported CPUs.
data.technical_explanation: AVX-512 has multiple feature subsets and vendor-specific availability.
common_misconceptions: Not every CPU with AVX-512 supports the same subsets.

data.definition: Fused Multiply-Add instruction extension.
data.short_explanation: It combines multiplication and addition with a single rounded operation.
data.technical_explanation: FMA instructions can improve numerical throughput in scientific and vector workloads.
common_misconceptions: FMA3 is not the same as AVX2.

data.definition: ARM SIMD instruction extension.
data.short_explanation: It accelerates vector arithmetic on ARM processors.
data.technical_explanation: NEON provides 128-bit vector operations for integer and floating-point data.
common_misconceptions: NEON and AVX are different instruction-set families.

data.definition: Reduced Instruction Set Computer design philosophy.
data.short_explanation: It emphasizes a relatively simple instruction set and regular execution model.
data.technical_explanation: Modern RISC CPUs still use sophisticated microarchitectural techniques internally.
common_misconceptions: RISC does not mean low performance.

data.definition: Complex Instruction Set Computer design philosophy.
data.short_explanation: It uses an instruction set with many operations and addressing modes.
data.technical_explanation: x86 is commonly classified as CISC at the ISA level while using RISC-like internal micro-operations.
common_misconceptions: CISC and RISC describe ISA philosophies, not raw performance.

data.definition: A major CPU instruction-set architecture family.
data.short_explanation: It powers most traditional PC processors.
data.technical_explanation: Modern x86 CPUs use complex decode and internal micro-operation mechanisms.
common_misconceptions: x86 is broader than x86-64.

data.definition: The 64-bit extension of the x86 architecture.
data.short_explanation: It is the dominant 64-bit PC ISA.
data.technical_explanation: x86-64 adds 64-bit registers and address space while retaining compatibility with legacy x86 instructions.
common_misconceptions: x86-64 does not mean every application uses 64-bit pointers everywhere.

data.definition: The 64-bit ARM instruction set architecture.
data.short_explanation: It is used by many modern mobile, embedded, and Apple processors.
data.technical_explanation: ARM64 uses the AArch64 instruction set and a load/store design.
common_misconceptions: ARM64 is an ISA, not one CPU design.

data.definition: An open-standard instruction set architecture.
data.short_explanation: It allows vendors to build processors around a modular open ISA.
data.technical_explanation: RISC-V defines base integer instructions and optional extensions.
common_misconceptions: RISC-V is not one specific CPU.

data.definition: Instruction Set Architecture.
data.short_explanation: The programmer-visible instruction and register interface of a CPU.
data.technical_explanation: The ISA defines instructions, registers, memory rules, and privilege behavior.
common_misconceptions: ISA is different from microarchitecture.

data.definition: The internal design used to implement an ISA.
data.short_explanation: Different CPUs can implement the same ISA with different internal designs.
data.technical_explanation: Microarchitecture includes pipelines, caches, execution units, branch predictors, and schedulers.
common_misconceptions: Microarchitecture is not the same as manufacturing process node.

data.definition: A semiconductor manufacturing technology generation.
data.short_explanation: Smaller process technologies can improve density or efficiency.
data.technical_explanation: Modern node names no longer correspond directly to one physical transistor dimension.
common_misconceptions: A smaller node does not automatically guarantee a faster chip.

data.definition: A semiconductor device used as a switch or amplifier.
data.short_explanation: Modern chips contain billions of transistors.
data.technical_explanation: CMOS transistors form logic gates, memory cells, and analog circuits.
common_misconceptions: More transistors do not automatically mean higher performance.

data.definition: A transistor architecture using a fin-shaped silicon channel.
data.short_explanation: It improves electrostatic control over older planar transistors.
data.technical_explanation: The gate wraps around multiple sides of the fin to reduce leakage.
common_misconceptions: FinFET and node names are not identical concepts.

data.definition: Gate-All-Around transistor architecture.
data.short_explanation: A transistor design surrounding the channel with the gate.
data.technical_explanation: GAA improves gate control and is used in newer process technologies.
common_misconceptions: GAA is a transistor structure, not a CPU architecture.

data.definition: A board carrying conductive traces and components.
data.short_explanation: It physically and electrically connects electronic components.
data.technical_explanation: A PCB uses copper layers, dielectric material, vias, and soldered components.
common_misconceptions: PCB is not synonymous with the entire computer.

data.definition: A conductive path on a PCB.
data.short_explanation: It carries a signal or power between components.
data.technical_explanation: Trace width, length, layer, and geometry affect resistance and signal integrity.
common_misconceptions: A trace is not a discrete wire outside the board.

data.definition: A plated hole connecting conductive PCB layers.
data.short_explanation: It lets signals and power move between board layers.
data.technical_explanation: Vias can be through, blind, or buried depending on board construction.
common_misconceptions: A via is not the same as a component lead.

data.definition: A large conductive PCB region serving as a reference and return path.
data.short_explanation: It helps power delivery and signal integrity.
data.technical_explanation: High-speed boards often place continuous ground planes beneath signal layers.
common_misconceptions: A ground plane is not always earth ground.

data.definition: The quality and reliability of electrical signals.
data.short_explanation: Good signal integrity keeps high-speed data recoverable.
data.technical_explanation: Loss, reflection, crosstalk, jitter, and impedance mismatch can degrade a link.
common_misconceptions: Signal integrity is not only about voltage level.

data.definition: The effective opposition of a circuit to changing signals.
data.short_explanation: Controlled impedance helps high-speed links remain stable.
data.technical_explanation: Transmission-line impedance depends on geometry and dielectric properties.
common_misconceptions: Impedance is not the same as DC resistance.

data.definition: Two conductors carrying complementary signal voltages.
data.short_explanation: It improves noise rejection on high-speed links.
data.technical_explanation: The receiver uses the voltage difference between the two conductors.
common_misconceptions: A differential pair is not one wire.

data.definition: Serializer/Deserializer.
data.short_explanation: It converts parallel data into high-speed serial streams and back.
data.technical_explanation: SerDes blocks drive and recover data on interfaces such as PCIe and Ethernet.
common_misconceptions: SerDes is an implementation block, not a connector.

data.definition: Four-level pulse-amplitude modulation.
data.short_explanation: It uses four signal levels to carry more bits per symbol.
data.technical_explanation: PAM4 is used in newer high-speed links to increase symbol efficiency.
common_misconceptions: PAM4 does not carry four bits per symbol.

data.definition: Non-Return-to-Zero binary signaling.
data.short_explanation: It uses two main signal levels.
data.technical_explanation: NRZ commonly carries one bit per symbol.
common_misconceptions: NRZ is a signaling scheme, not a protocol.

data.definition: Forward Error Correction.
data.short_explanation: It adds redundant information so some transmission errors can be corrected.
data.technical_explanation: FEC reduces the need for retransmission on high-speed links.
common_misconceptions: FEC adds some overhead.

data.definition: Bit Error Rate.
data.short_explanation: The fraction of bits received incorrectly.
data.technical_explanation: It is a key measure of link quality and signal integrity.
common_misconceptions: A BER result depends on test length and conditions.

data.definition: GigaTransfers per second.
data.short_explanation: A unit for serial link transfer events.
data.technical_explanation: It measures signaling events rather than usable bytes per second.
common_misconceptions: GT/s is not the same as GB/s.

data.definition: Gigabytes per second.
data.short_explanation: A data transfer rate in bytes.
data.technical_explanation: It is often used for memory and storage throughput.
common_misconceptions: GB/s and Gb/s differ by a factor of eight before overhead.

data.definition: Gigabits per second.
data.short_explanation: A data transfer rate in bits.
data.technical_explanation: Networks commonly advertise speeds in gigabits per second.
common_misconceptions: Gb/s is not GB/s.

data.definition: The delay between an action and a result.
data.short_explanation: Lower latency generally improves responsiveness.
data.technical_explanation: Latency can come from computation, memory, networking, storage, and display stages.
common_misconceptions: Latency is different from bandwidth.

data.definition: The amount of useful work or data completed per unit time.
data.short_explanation: It measures total rate of completion.
data.technical_explanation: Throughput depends on bandwidth, concurrency, protocol overhead, and bottlenecks.
common_misconceptions: Peak throughput is not the same as sustained throughput.

data.definition: A limiting stage that caps overall performance.
data.short_explanation: The slowest relevant stage constrains the system.
data.technical_explanation: Bottlenecks can occur in CPU, GPU, memory, storage, software, or networking.
common_misconceptions: The bottleneck can change with workload and settings.

data.definition: Reducing component performance to stay within a thermal limit.
data.short_explanation: It protects hardware from excessive temperature.
data.technical_explanation: Firmware can lower clocks or voltage when thermal limits are reached.
common_misconceptions: A high temperature does not always mean throttling is active.

data.definition: The highest reported temperature inside a component region.
data.short_explanation: It reveals localized heating.
data.technical_explanation: GPU and other chips can report hotspot or junction temperatures separately from edge temperatures.
common_misconceptions: Hotspot and average temperature are different readings.

data.definition: The hottest or modeled internal semiconductor temperature.
data.short_explanation: It is an important thermal safety metric.
data.technical_explanation: Sensors may estimate the hottest point inside the die rather than measuring the package surface.
common_misconceptions: Junction temperature is not the same as heatsink temperature.

data.definition: The temperature of the surrounding environment.
data.short_explanation: It influences achievable component temperatures.
data.technical_explanation: Cooling systems operate relative to the temperature of the air or liquid they reject heat into.
common_misconceptions: A cooler cannot normally cool below ambient without refrigeration.

data.definition: The temperature difference between a component and its environment.
data.short_explanation: It helps compare cooling independent of room temperature.
data.technical_explanation: Delta-T is often component temperature minus ambient temperature.
common_misconceptions: Lower absolute temperature can simply reflect a colder room.

data.definition: Sound produced by operating hardware.
data.short_explanation: Lower noise makes a system quieter.
data.technical_explanation: Fans, pumps, coils, and mechanical drives can all contribute to acoustic output.
common_misconceptions: Noise perception depends on frequency as well as level.

data.definition: Audible vibration from inductors or other power components.
data.short_explanation: It can produce a high-pitched electrical sound.
data.technical_explanation: Changing magnetic forces can physically vibrate coils under varying load.
common_misconceptions: Coil whine does not automatically mean hardware is failing.

data.definition: Voltage Regulator Module.
data.short_explanation: Circuitry that converts and regulates power for a component.
data.technical_explanation: A VRM uses switching devices, inductors, capacitors, and a controller.
common_misconceptions: More phases alone do not guarantee better VRM performance.

data.definition: A semiconductor switching device used in power electronics.
data.short_explanation: It switches current in VRMs and power supplies.
data.technical_explanation: Power MOSFETs rapidly switch current to regulate voltage efficiently.
common_misconceptions: MOSFET current rating is not a complete measure of VRM quality.

data.definition: An integrated driver and MOSFET power stage.
data.short_explanation: It combines several VRM functions in one package.
data.technical_explanation: A DrMOS commonly integrates high-side and low-side switches and a driver.
common_misconceptions: Higher advertised current does not guarantee better real-world power delivery.

data.definition: A magnetic energy-storage component used in power converters.
data.short_explanation: It smooths current in VRMs and PSUs.
data.technical_explanation: Inductors resist rapid current changes and work with switches and capacitors.
common_misconceptions: Size alone does not define inductor quality.

data.definition: A component that stores electrical charge.
data.short_explanation: It smooths voltage and supports transient response.
data.technical_explanation: Capacitor type, capacitance, ESR, and ripple rating matter in power circuits.
common_misconceptions: More capacitance does not automatically mean better power delivery.

data.definition: PCI Express 1.0 generation detail
data.short_explanation: A PCIe {i} generation defines a set of link and transport capabilities.
data.technical_explanation: It specifies signaling, link training, compatibility, and performance rules.
common_misconceptions: The generation alone does not specify lane width.
